front_blocks.md: Define **ion**.

back_blocks.md: An **ion** is an electrically charged atom or group of atoms formed by the loss or gain of **electrons**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Atoms gain or lose electrons to achieve a full outer shell.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Atoms lose or gain electrons so that their outer shell becomes full, giving them a stable electronic structure like a **noble gas**.

front_blocks.md: What is the difference between a **cation** and an **anion**?

back_blocks.md: A **cation** is a positively charged ion formed when an atom loses electrons. An **anion** is a negatively charged ion formed when an atom gains electrons.

front_blocks.md: When a sodium atom loses one electron, it forms a **..........** charged ion with the electronic structure of **..........** .

back_blocks.md: When a sodium atom loses one electron, it forms a **positively** charged ion with the electronic structure of **neon**.

front_blocks.md: Define **cation**.

back_blocks.md: A **cation** is a positively charged ion formed when an atom loses **electrons**, leaving it with more **protons** than **electrons**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Non-metals lose electrons to form positive ions.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Non-metals gain electrons to form **negatively** charged ions (**anions**). It is metals that lose electrons to form positive ions.

front_blocks.md: How does the charge on an ion relate to the number of electrons lost or gained?

back_blocks.md: The charge equals the number of electrons lost or gained. For example, losing 2 electrons gives a 2+ charge and gaining 1 electron gives a 1− charge.

front_blocks.md: Which noble gas has the same electronic structure as a chloride ion?

back_blocks.md: A **chloride ion** has the same electronic structure as **argon**, having gained one electron to fill its outer shell.

front_blocks.md: Define **compound ion**.

front_blocks.md: Why do ionic compounds have no overall charge?

back_blocks.md: Ionic compounds have no overall charge because the positive charges of the cations are exactly cancelled by the negative charges of the **anions**.

back_blocks.md: The formula is FeSO<sub>4</sub>. Fe<sup>2+</sup> and SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> have equal and opposite charges that cancel directly, so one of each ion is needed.

front_blocks.md: Describe the **swap-and-drop method** for writing ionic formulae.

back_blocks.md: The **swap-and-drop method** involves swapping the sizes of the ion charges and using them as the subscript numbers in the formula, then simplifying to the lowest whole number ratio.

front_blocks.md: What does a dot-and-cross diagram show for an ionic compound?

back_blocks.md: It shows the **transfer of electrons** from a metal atom to a non-metal atom, using dots and crosses to represent electrons from each atom.

back_blocks.md: In a dot-and-cross diagram for an ionic compound, each ion is enclosed in **square brackets** and the charge is shown in **superscript** outside the brackets.

front_blocks.md: In the dot-and-cross diagram for NaCl, how many electrons are transferred and in which direction?

back_blocks.md: One electron is transferred from the outer shell of the **sodium** atom to the outer shell of the **chlorine** atom, forming Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>-</sup>.

front_blocks.md: Describe a **dot-and-cross diagram**.

back_blocks.md: A **dot-and-cross diagram** is a representation of bonding that uses dots and crosses to distinguish **electrons** from different atoms, showing how they are transferred or shared.

In the dot-and-cross diagram for MgO, both atoms lose electrons.

**Magnesium loses** two electrons and **oxygen gains** two electrons. Electron transfer is always from metal to non-metal.

back_blocks.md: Students must be able to draw diagrams for combinations of elements from **Groups 1, 2 and 3** (metals) and **Groups 5, 6 and 7** (non-metals).

back_blocks.md: Different symbols (dots and crosses) are used to make it clear which electrons came from which atom, showing that **electron transfer** has occurred.

front_blocks.md: Define **ionic bonding**.

back_blocks.md: **Ionic bonding** is the strong electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged **ions**, acting in all directions in an ionic compound.

cards.front_md: Define **ionic bonding**.
cards.back_md: **Ionic bonding** is the strong electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged **ions**, acting in all directions in an ionic compound.

front_blocks.md: What is a **giant ionic lattice**?

back_blocks.md: A **giant ionic lattice** is a regular three-dimensional arrangement of thousands of alternating positive and negative ions held together by strong electrostatic forces in all directions.

cards.front_md: What is a **giant ionic lattice**?
cards.back_md: A **giant ionic lattice** is a regular three-dimensional arrangement of thousands of alternating positive and negative ions held together by strong electrostatic forces in all directions.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Ionic compounds conduct electricity in the solid state.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
In the solid state, **ions are in fixed positions** in the lattice and cannot move, so they cannot carry a charge or conduct electricity.

cards.front_md:
**True or False?**

Ionic compounds conduct electricity in the solid state.
cards.back_md:
**False.**

In the solid state, **ions are in fixed positions** in the lattice and cannot move, so they cannot carry a charge or conduct electricity.

front_blocks.md: Ionic compounds have high melting points because the **..........** forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions require a large amount of **..........** to overcome.

back_blocks.md: Ionic compounds have high melting points because the **electrostatic** forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions require a large amount of **thermal energy** to overcome.

cards.front_md: Ionic compounds have high melting points because the **..........** forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions require a large amount of **..........** to overcome.
cards.back_md: Ionic compounds have high melting points because the **electrostatic** forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions require a large amount of **thermal energy** to overcome.

front_blocks.md: Why do ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water?

back_blocks.md: When molten or dissolved, the **ions** are free to move and can carry a charge, allowing electrical current to flow.

cards.front_md: Why do ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water?
cards.back_md: When molten or dissolved, the **ions** are free to move and can carry a charge, allowing electrical current to flow.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
MgO has a higher melting point than NaCl because Mg<sup>2+</sup> and O<sup>2-</sup> ions have greater charges than Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>-</sup> ions.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Higher ion charges produce stronger electrostatic forces. MgO contains 2+ and 2− ions, so more energy is needed to overcome its **giant ionic lattice** compared to NaCl.

cards.front_md:
**True or False?**

MgO has a higher melting point than NaCl because Mg<sup>2+</sup> and O<sup>2-</sup> ions have greater charges than Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>-</sup> ions.
cards.back_md:
**True.**

Higher ion charges produce stronger electrostatic forces. MgO contains 2+ and 2− ions, so more energy is needed to overcome its **giant ionic lattice** compared to NaCl.

front_blocks.md: In an ionic compound, the ions are tightly packed in a **..........** arrangement with strong electrostatic forces acting in **..........** directions.

back_blocks.md: In an ionic compound, the ions are tightly packed in a **regular** arrangement with strong electrostatic forces acting in **all** directions.

cards.front_md: In an ionic compound, the ions are tightly packed in a **..........** arrangement with strong electrostatic forces acting in **..........** directions.
cards.back_md: In an ionic compound, the ions are tightly packed in a **regular** arrangement with strong electrostatic forces acting in **all** directions.

front_blocks.md: What carries the charge when an ionic compound conducts electricity?

back_blocks.md: The **ions** carry the charge. Electrons do not move through ionic compounds — it is the movement of free ions that allows conduction.

cards.front_md: What carries the charge when an ionic compound conducts electricity?
cards.back_md: The **ions** carry the charge. Electrons do not move through ionic compounds — it is the movement of free ions that allows conduction.

front_blocks.md: How does increasing the charge on the ions in an ionic compound affect its melting point?

back_blocks.md: Increasing the ion charges strengthens the **electrostatic forces of attraction**, so more energy is needed to break the lattice and the **melting point** is higher.

cards.front_md: How does increasing the charge on the ions in an ionic compound affect its melting point?
cards.back_md: Increasing the ion charges strengthens the **electrostatic forces of attraction**, so more energy is needed to break the lattice and the **melting point** is higher.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Electrostatic forces in ionic compounds only act between neighbouring ions.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Electrostatic forces in ionic compounds act in **all directions**, not just between immediate neighbours, which is why the **giant ionic lattice** is so stable.

cards.front_md:

cards.back_md:

Electrostatic forces in ionic compounds act in **all directions**, not just between immediate neighbours, which is why the **giant ionic lattice** is so stable.
